fixes.explanation: You got it, baker. The verse says it plainly: "…the Day of the LORD is near." Then it describes that day as "…a day of clouds, a time of doom for the nations." Right before that, God tells Ezekiel to say, "Wail, 'Alas for that day!'" (Ezekiel 30:2).
Right, baker. The verse says the day "…will be a day of clouds, a time of doom for the nations." Doom is the opposite of peace. So False is the answer, and the verse backs it up.
Yes, baker. The verse says "…there will be anguish in Cush when the slain fall in Egypt…" Cush is Egypt's neighbor to the south. Anguish is the word God gives for Cush in that moment.
I know, friend, when a big neighbor falls, you might expect a celebration. But the verse says the opposite. When the slain fall in Egypt, "…there will be anguish in Cush…" That's a heavy moment.
That's the word, baker. God says, "…her proud strength will collapse." The verse puts that right alongside the fall of Egypt's allies. Picture a tall stack of cookie boxes coming down.

Exactly, baker. God says, "Then they will know that I am the LORD…" when He sets fire to Egypt and her helpers are shattered. That line comes back again and again in this chapter. So the answer is that they will know He is the LORD.

Wealth does come up in this chapter, baker, but not here. The verse says the messengers go out "…to frighten Cush out of complacency." Earlier it says Egypt's wealth is taken away (Ezekiel 30:4). This verse says nothing about carrying off the wealth of Cush.
Close on the water, friend, but the direction is the other way. God says, "I will make the streams dry up…" Not overflow, but dry up. Nothing is rushing in here, it's all going away.

Good guess for a royal kind of word, friend, but it's not this verse. God says, "By the hands of foreigners I will bring desolation upon the land and everything in it." A prince comes up in a later verse, and not in a good way. God says there will no longer be a prince in Egypt (Ezekiel 30:13).
I'd love to give you that one, baker. But the verse says something else. God says, "…I will instill fear in that land." The verse doesn't mention hope.

That's right, baker. God says, "…I have broken the arm of Pharaoh king of Egypt." He adds that it "…has not been bound up for healing, or splinted for strength to hold the sword." So the answer is his arm.

I get the guess, friend, but this verse is about something else. God says, "…I have broken the arm of Pharaoh king of Egypt." The verse speaks of a splint for strength "…to hold the sword," and it's the arm that's named.

I see where you're headed, baker, but the verse points somewhere else. God says, "…I have broken the arm of Pharaoh king of Egypt." It mentions a splint for strength "…to hold the sword," and the arm is what's named.

That's right, baker. God says He "…will make the sword fall from his hand." It ties back to the arm that had not been splinted "…for strength to hold the sword." Without strong arms, that sword isn't staying in his hand.
That's right, baker. God says He will break the arms of Pharaoh, "…who will groan before him like a mortally wounded man." I think this one is a heavy picture.
